evidence.note: Early analysis identifies the dominant cost consumer: data-dependent gather of tree values limited to 2 loads/cycle, over batch_size=256; enumerates slot limits (alu:12, valu:6, load:2) and VLEN=8, and frames the 147,734→<1250 (118x) target. Rough identification of the bottleneck, not yet a floor.

Quantitative fragments: 'load_offset gather, 8 per chunk, limited by 2 loads/cycle = 4 cycles per chunk' and 'valu hash: 6 stages, 3 ops each' — per-operation cost estimates, edging toward a cost model but never summed into a total bundle count or lower bound.

Reasons about exploiting ≤32 distinct indices in rounds 0-4/10-14 to broadcast tree values instead of 256 gathers, i.e. roughly how a transform saves cycles — anchor-5 'reason roughly about how much a transform can save'.

The agent was trapped in a stuck bash-heredoc loop for the entire middle/end and never ran run_tests.sh on an optimized kernel, so no measured cycle count ever existed to compare against a floor; the cost reasoning stayed theoretical and was never operationalized into gap-to-floor prioritization.

reasoning: The agent clearly identifies the dominant cycle consumers (per-round gather × batch, bounded by 2 loads/cycle) and reasons roughly about how transforms like broadcasting few-distinct-index rounds save cycles, matching anchor 5. A few quantitative fragments (chunk cycles, hash op counts) push slightly beyond hand-waving, but it never constructs an explicit end-to-end instruction-count/slot-occupancy cost model, never estimates a coherent theoretical lower bound, and — being stuck in a heredoc loop — never used a measured-vs-floor gap to direct optimization, keeping it below anchor 8.
